## Introduction
Employees’ overall workplace ratings may be associated with how their organization handles complaints, provides learning opportunities, and awards pay increases based on performance. This report examines whether learning opportunities and performance-based raises explain additional variation in overall ratings beyond complaint handling alone.

## Workflow
The analysis follows a complete linear regression workflow:
**Explore Data → Specify Models → Estimate Models → Compare Models → Evaluate Assumptions → Select a Model → Interpret Results**

## Overview of the Models
Four nested regression models are compared to examine whether learning opportunities and performance-based raises explain additional variation in overall workplace ratings beyond complaint handling.

| Model | Formula | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **M0: Null** | `rating ~ 1` | Establish a baseline using only the mean overall rating |
| **M1: Complaints** | `rating ~ complaints` | Examine the association between complaint handling and overall ratings |
| **M2: + Learning** | `rating ~ complaints + learning` | Assess whether learning opportunities explain additional variation beyond complaint handling |
| **M3: + Raises** | `rating ~ complaints + learning + raises` | Assess whether performance-based raises explain further variation beyond complaint handling and learning |

The models are nested: each successive model retains all predictors from the preceding model and adds one predictor.

## Dataset
R Core Team. (n.d.). *The Chatterjee–Price attitude data*. R documentation. https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/attitude.html

## 1. Load packages and prepare the setup
```{r}
library(carData)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(performance)
library(gt)
```

### Keep the same complete-case sample for every model
```{r}
dat <- attitude |>
  select(rating, complaints, learning, raises)

n <- nrow(dat)
```
The analysis includes **`r n` departments**.

## Research Question and Prediction
How are favorable evaluations of complaint handling, learning opportunities, and performance-based raises associated with overall workplace ratings? Do learning opportunities and performance-based raises explain additional variation beyond complaint handling alone?

I expect favorable evaluations of complaint handling to be positively associated with overall workplace ratings, because effective responses to employee concerns may reflect a supportive work environment. I also expect favorable evaluations of learning opportunities and performance-based raises to explain additional variation in overall ratings, as these aspects may reflect opportunities for development and recognition of employee contributions.

## 2. Explore the data
### Descriptive statistics
```{r}
#| label: descriptive-table
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for workplace attitude variables"
descriptives <- dat |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(rating, complaints, learning, raises),
      list(mean = mean, sd = sd, min = min, max = max)
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
    names_sep = "_"
  )

descriptives |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 2)
```

### Distribution of rating
Overall workplace ratings are concentrated around 60 to 75% favorable responses, with a peak near 65%. The distribution has a longer lower tail, with several departments reporting less favorable overall ratings.
```{r}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 15,
    fill = "#669BBC",
    color = "white",
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_density(
    linewidth = 0.9,
    color = "#9A3038"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Rating score",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### Relationships between predictors and rating
Favorable evaluations of complaint handling show a strong, approximately linear positive association with overall workplace ratings. This pattern is consistent with the prediction that departments with more positively evaluated complaint handling tend to receive higher overall ratings.
```{r}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = complaints, y = rating)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "#27638A"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Complaint handling (% favorable)",
    y = "Overall workplace rating (% favorable)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### Relationship between learning and rating
Favorable evaluations of learning opportunities show a positive, approximately linear association with overall workplace ratings, although the points are more dispersed than in the complaint-handling plot. This supports the expected positive relationship, but does not establish whether learning explains additional variation beyond complaint handling.
```{r}
#| label: learning-scatterplot
#| fig-cap: "Relationship between learning and rating"

ggplot(dat, aes(x = learning, y = rating)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "#27638A"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Learning opportunities (% favorable)",
    y = "Overall workplace rating (% favorable)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## 3. Specify and estimate competing models
The models are **nested**: each successive model contains all predictors from the preceding model, plus one or more additional predictors.
```{r}
# Null: Intercept-only model
mod0 <- lm(rating ~ 1, data = dat)

# Complaints model
mod1 <- lm(rating ~ complaints, data = dat)

# Complaints + learning model
mod2 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning, data = dat)

# Expanded model
mod3 <- lm(rating ~ complaints + learning + raises, data = dat)
```

### Inspecting the models
The complaints coefficient represents the unadjusted association with overall ratings in M1, the association controlling for learning in M2, and the association controlling for both learning and raises in M3. Its estimate decreases from `r round(coef(mod1)[["complaints"]], 3)` in M1 to `r round(coef(mod2)[["complaints"]], 3)` in M2 and remains similar at `r round(coef(mod3)[["complaints"]], 3)` in M3. Complaint handling remains positively and statistically significantly associated with overall ratings across all three models.
```{r}
summary(mod0)
summary(mod1)
summary(mod2)
summary(mod3)

confint(mod3)
```

## 4. Compare the models

We evaluate the models using two complementary approaches.

**Nested-model F-tests** determine whether the additional predictor(s) in a larger model produce a statistically significant improvement in fit.

**Overall model performance** describes how well each model fits the observed data.

Our main performance metrics are:

- **R²:** Proportion of variation explained.
- **Adjusted R²:** Explained variation adjusted for model complexity.
- **RMSE:** Root mean squared error, expressed in rating-score units.
- **ΔR²:** Increase in explained variation compared with the preceding model.

### 4.1. Conduct nested-model comparisons
Adding complaint handling significantly improved model fit relative to the intercept-only model (p < .001). Adding learning opportunities did not significantly improve fit beyond complaint handling (p = .135), and performance-based raises provided no significant further improvement (p = .877).
```{r}
#| label: nested-tests
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)
tests
```

Each row represents a model. The F-statistic and p-value on each row after the first test whether that model improves fit relative to the preceding model.

For example:

- M1 versus M0 tests the contribution of complaint handling.
- M2 versus M1 tests the additional contribution of learning opportunities beyond complaint handling.
- M3 versus M2 tests the additional contribution of performance-based raises beyond complaint handling and learning opportunities.

We can retain and rename the statistics relevant to our comparison table.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-nested-tests
tests <- tests |>
  select(Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`) |>
  rename(
    Residual.df = Res.Df,
    Nested.Df = Df,
    Nested.F.stat = F,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>F)`
  )
```

### 4.2. Extract overall model performance
The `glance()` function returns a one-row data frame containing model-level statistics.
We can apply it to each fitted model.

```{r}
#| label: extract-model-metrics
glance0 <- glance(mod0)
glance1 <- glance(mod1)
glance2 <- glance(mod2)
glance3 <- glance(mod3)
```

We can then combine these results using `rbind()`.
```{r}
#| label: combine-model-metrics

mods <- c(
  "M0: Null",
  "M1: Complaints",
  "M2: + Learning",
  "M3: + Raises"
)

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2,
  glance3
)
```

### 4.3. Combine nested tests and model performance
Because the rows in `glances` and `tests` represent the same models in the same order, we can combine them using `cbind()`.

```{r}
#| label: combine-comparisons
comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests
)
```

Next, calculate the change in R² between successive models using `lag()`.
We will also calculate RMSE directly from each model's residuals.
```{r}
#| label: prepare-comparison-table

comparison_table <- comparison_table |>
  mutate(
    Delta.R2 = r.squared - lag(r.squared),

    RMSE = c(
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod0)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod1)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod2)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod3)^2))
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Model,
    r.squared,
    Delta.R2,
    adj.r.squared,
    RMSE,
    Residual.df,
    Nested.Df,
    Nested.F.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  )
```

**Why calculate RMSE separately?**

Although `glance()` provides a statistic called `sigma`, this is the residual standard error rather than the ordinary in-sample RMSE. The two use different denominators.

For consistency, we calculate RMSE explicitly as the square root of the mean squared residual.

### 4.4. Display the combined model-comparison table

```{r}
#| label: model-comparison-table
#| tbl-cap: "Overall model performance and incremental nested-model comparisons"
comparison_table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    r.squared = "R²",
    Delta.R2 = "ΔR²",
    adj.r.squared = "Adjusted R²",
    RMSE = "RMSE",
    Residual.df = "Residual df",
    Nested.Df = "Nested df",
    Nested.F.stat = "Nested F",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      r.squared,
      Delta.R2,
      adj.r.squared,
      RMSE,
      Nested.F.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Delta.R2, Nested.Df, Nested.F.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )
```

### Interpreting the combined table
M3 explained the largest proportion of variation in overall workplace ratings (R² = `r round(comparison_table$r.squared[4], 4)`), although its advantage over M2 was negligible. Adjusted R² increased from `r round(comparison_table$adj.r.squared[2], 3)` in M1 to `r round(comparison_table$adj.r.squared[3], 3)` in M2, then decreased to `r round(comparison_table$adj.r.squared[4], 3)` in M3. Adding complaint handling explained `r round(100 * comparison_table$Delta.R2[2], 1)`% of the total variation and significantly improved fit (p < .001), while reducing RMSE from `r round(comparison_table$RMSE[1], 2)` to `r round(comparison_table$RMSE[2], 2)` percentage points—a substantial improvement relative to the baseline. Adding learning opportunities explained a further `r round(100 * comparison_table$Delta.R2[3], 2)` percentage points of variance, but the improvement was not statistically significant (p = `r sprintf("%.3f", comparison_table$Nested.p.value[3])`). Its RMSE reduction of `r round(comparison_table$RMSE[2] - comparison_table$RMSE[3], 2)` percentage points appears modest. Adding performance-based raises explained only another `r round(100 * comparison_table$Delta.R2[4], 2)` percentage points of variance (p = `r sprintf("%.3f", comparison_table$Nested.p.value[4])`) and reduced RMSE by just `r round(comparison_table$RMSE[3] - comparison_table$RMSE[4], 3)` percentage points, an improvement that appears practically negligible. Overall, complaint handling provided the clearest explanatory contribution; learning offered a modest but uncertain additional contribution, whereas raises added little beyond the other predictors.

### 4.5. Additional performance comparison
The `performance` package also provides a convenient way to compare fitted models.

```{r}
#| label: performance-comparison
#| results: hide
performance_comparison <- compare_performance(
  mod0,
  mod1,
  mod2,
  mod3,
  rank = TRUE
)
```

In the Console, inspect:
```{r}
performance_comparison
plot(performance_comparison)
```

## 5. Select a provisional model
M2, which includes complaint handling and learning opportunities, was provisionally selected because it had the highest adjusted R² and a slightly lower RMSE than M1. However, adding learning did not significantly improve model fit, so M1 remains a plausible, simpler alternative. M3 offered negligible additional explained variance and a lower adjusted R² than M2, providing little justification for including raises. Diagnostic findings will inform the final model selection.

```{r}
#| label: select-model
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Model == "M2: + Learning")

selected_name <- selected_row$Model
selected_model <- mod2
```

The provisionally selected model is **`r selected_name`**.

Its performance is:

- R² = **`r round(selected_row$r.squared, 3)`**
- Adjusted R² = **`r round(selected_row$adj.r.squared, 3)`**
- In-sample RMSE = **`r round(selected_row$RMSE, 2)` percentage points** of favourable overall workplace ratings.

We next examine the model's diagnostic plots and multicollinearity to assess potential limitations.

## 6. Evaluate regression diagnostics
The residuals-versus-fitted plot showed no pronounced curvature, suggesting that the linear specification was broadly reasonable. However, the Q–Q plot showed departures from normality, and the scale–location plot suggested uneven residual variability, particularly greater variability at lower fitted values. Department 24 had relatively high leverage and warrants further inspection, although no observations exceeded the displayed Cook’s distance = .5 contours.
```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Regression diagnostic plots for M2"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(selected_model)
par(op)
```

Multicollinearity was low, with VIF values of 1.55 for both predictors. These findings do not rule out M2, but the small sample and potential heteroscedasticity warrant caution when interpreting conventional p-values and confidence intervals, particularly for the uncertain additional contribution of learning.
```{r}
#| label: collinearity
check_collinearity(selected_model)
```


## 7. Select and report the preferred model
### 7.1. Model selection
M2 was selected as the preferred model because it had the highest adjusted R² and a modestly lower RMSE than M1, while allowing the association between learning opportunities and overall ratings to be examined after accounting for complaint handling. However, the additional contribution of learning was small and did not reach statistical significance, so M1 remains a defensible, simpler alternative. M3 was not selected because raises contributed negligible additional explained variance and reduced adjusted R². Diagnostics for M2 showed no pronounced curvature and low multicollinearity, but suggested departures from residual normality, uneven residual variability, and a high-leverage observation. M2 is therefore retained with caution, particularly regarding the uncertain contribution of learning.

```{r}
#| label: final-model-selection
selected_model <- mod2

selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  filter(Model == "M2: + Learning")

selected_name <- selected_row$Model
```

### 7.2. Regression coefficient table
```{r}
#| label: coefficient-table
#| tbl-cap: "Unstandardized regression coefficients for M2"
coefficient_results <- tidy(
  selected_model,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95
)

coefficient_results |>
  select(
    term, estimate, std.error,
    conf.low, conf.high, p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    term = "Predictor",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    std.error = "SE",
    conf.low = "95% CI lower",
    conf.high = "95% CI upper",
    p.value = "p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      estimate, std.error,
      conf.low, conf.high
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
    }
  )
```

### 7.3. Interpreting the coefficients
Holding favorable evaluations of learning opportunities constant, a one-percentage-point increase in favorable evaluations of complaint handling was associated with a **`r round(coefficient_results |> filter(term == "complaints") |> pull(estimate), 2)`-percentage-point** increase in predicted favorable overall workplace ratings, 95% CI [`r round(coefficient_results |> filter(term == "complaints") |> pull(conf.low), 2)`, `r round(coefficient_results |> filter(term == "complaints") |> pull(conf.high), 2)`], p < .001. The confidence interval excluded zero, supporting a positive conditional association.

Holding favorable evaluations of complaint handling constant, a one-percentage-point increase in favorable evaluations of learning opportunities was associated with an estimated **`r round(coefficient_results |> filter(term == "learning") |> pull(estimate), 2)`-percentage-point** increase in predicted favorable overall ratings, 95% CI [`r round(coefficient_results |> filter(term == "learning") |> pull(conf.low), 2)`, `r round(coefficient_results |> filter(term == "learning") |> pull(conf.high), 2)`], p = `r sprintf("%.3f", coefficient_results |> filter(term == "learning") |> pull(p.value))`. This interval included zero, indicating uncertainty about the direction and magnitude of learning's conditional association. These conventional confidence intervals and p-values should be interpreted cautiously given the diagnostic concerns.

### 7.4. Overall model performance
The selected model, **`r selected_name`**, explained approximately **`r round(100 * selected_row$r.squared, 1)`%** of the variation in department-level overall workplace ratings (R² = **`r round(selected_row$r.squared, 3)`**). Its adjusted R² was **`r round(selected_row$adj.r.squared, 3)`**, accounting for model complexity. Its in-sample RMSE was **`r round(selected_row$RMSE, 2)` percentage points**, describing the root-mean-square discrepancy between observed and fitted percentages of favorable overall ratings. These statistics describe fit within the current sample and do not establish predictive accuracy for new departments.


## 8. Discussion and limitations
Complaint handling showed the clearest association with overall workplace ratings. Departments with more favorable evaluations of complaint handling tended to receive higher overall ratings, even after accounting for learning opportunities. Learning showed a positive estimated association, but its confidence interval included zero and its addition produced only a modest improvement in model fit. Performance-based raises added almost no explanatory value beyond complaint handling and learning. Thus, these data provide stronger evidence for the contribution of complaint handling than for the additional contributions of learning or raises.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The observational design does not establish causality, and department-level associations cannot be assumed to describe individual employees. The sample contained only 30 departments from one organization, limiting precision and generalizability. The measures came from the same survey, so shared response tendencies may partly explain their associations. Diagnostic plots also suggested departures from residual normality, uneven residual variability, and a high-leverage observation, warranting caution when interpreting conventional confidence intervals and p-values. Finally, incremental contributions depend on the order in which predictors were entered, and in-sample fit does not establish predictive accuracy for new departments. The uncertain findings for learning and raises therefore should not be interpreted as evidence that these workplace features are unimportant.
